water balance residual +1.5 TPH (feed 67.9, steam 65.4, level slope -0.01 %/min vs expected +0.90).

facts.detail: water balance residual +1.5 TPH (feed 67.9, steam 65.4, level slope -0.01 %/min vs expected +0.90): measured inflow exceeds what the drum level shows -> water is being lost between the feed meter and the drum (leak, blowdown passing), or the level reading is false

hypotheses.cause: Fireside erosion of a water wall tube by circulating bed material in the high-velocity bed-to-freeboard transition zone, progressively thinning the wall until it split longitudinally; internal deposits contributed by raising local metal temperature. Systemic: a foreseeable wear-out mechanism with no thickness-monitoring task, wear shields removed without engineering review, and an uncontrolled operating envelope (excess air, bed height, ash abrasiveness).
hypotheses.discriminator: Rising feed-water-to-steam ratio (feed 2-3 t/h over steam) WITH boiler-water conductivity FALLING - the circuit is being diluted, which establishes a pressure-part leak and excludes every non-leak explanation of the water imbalance. Go observe (not in the six tags): boiler-water conductivity trend (falling = leak; rising = concentration / feed-control fault; a large CBD loss would also lower it); make-up water consumption rate; furnace listening check for a hissing steam leak; furnace draught stability (here fluctuating); local vs sharp bed temperature drop near the leak; whether drum level can still be held on one BFP. At inspection the fracture morphology (thin-lipped longitudinal split at a broadly thinned zone) confirms erosion over overheating or corrosion.

hypotheses.cause: Total loss of fuel input from a degraded connection on one phase of the MCC incomer producing single-phasing, tripping all six coal feeder VFDs on phase loss. Systemic: all six feeders on one un-segregated bus section (a single-point-of-failure), and an electrical PM programme with no thermography and no connection-torque verification.
hypotheses.discriminator: All six feeder drives reporting an incoming supply abnormality (phase loss / under-voltage) at the same instant. Simultaneity across six independent mechanical drives is near-conclusive for a supply-side common cause, and the VFD fault-code content separates it from a process interlock, an operator stop and a drive-internal fault. Go observe (not in the six tags): the six VFD fault codes and their timestamps; the MCC incomer protection operation in the electrical event log; absence of any preceding bed temperature / drum level / furnace pressure excursion (process interlocks leave a clear trend trace); PA fan status (here running normally); DCS operator command logs (no stop command). Distinguish from a fuel hang-up (Case 6) by the step-vs-ramp onset and by all compartments falling equally rather than compartment-selectively.

hypotheses.cause: Seat leakage of the attemperator spray control valve (passing in the closed position), unmasked by a sharp turbine load increase in which firing rate and air flow lagged and the drum swelled. Systemic: no periodic passing / seat-tightness test for the spray valve, no boiler-friendly TG load ramp-rate limit, and a defect-reporting culture that left a known passing valve unlogged.
hypotheses.discriminator: Spray flow registered while spray demand is zero and the controller output is closed - a passing spray control valve, which no other hypothesis explains. Go observe (not in the six tags): attemperator spray flow vs spray demand and valve position; audible knocking / hammering in the main steam line near the stop valve; turbine differential expansion trend (here negative); saturated- and main-steam sample conductivity (here rising = moisture carry-over); combustion air flow and O2 for the new firing rate (here air on the low end, O2 below 2%); SH tube metal temperature falling with steam temperature.

hypotheses.cause: Two independent failures in sequence: PA fan motor winding overheating from coal-dust fouling of the cooling air passages tripped the running fan, and a defective run feed-back contact aborted the standby PA fan auto-start. hypotheses.discriminator: Divergence between motor WINDING temperature (rising over ~30 min) and motor CURRENT (normal): an overload would raise current with temperature, an electrical fault would trip protection first, so a winding-temperature rise alone identifies loss of the cooling air path. Go observe (not in the six tags): PA fan motor winding temperature vs motor current trend; standby PA fan auto-start command present with no run feed-back (the hidden second failure); PA header pressure collapse and loss of primary air; all coal feeders tripping simultaneously on the designed PA-fan-trip interlock; erratic bed temperature indication and low furnace draught after fluidising air is lost. On the six averaged tags this looks the same as a total feeder loss (Case 14).

hypotheses.discriminator: Confined to one compartment - the six-tag averages barely move. Go observe: PA flow to the affected compartment LOW while the PA header pressure stays NORMAL (isolates the restriction to that branch and excludes a fan/header cause); glowing hot material and rising surface temperature on the vertical portion of that PA line; erratic, non-uniform bed temperature in that one compartment only; bed differential pressure normal on all compartments (rules out excessive bed height); the bed ash drain valve verified closed and cold; the maintenance record showing recent work on that line with no damper restoration check.

hypotheses.cause: Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. hypotheses.discriminator: Not visible in the six process tags except a slow bed-temperature drift over WEEKS (less effective primary air reaches the bed). Systemic: a foreseeable wear-out mechanism with no thickness-monitoring task, wear shields removed without engineering review, and an uncontrolled operating envelope (excess air, bed height, ash abrasiveness).
hypotheses.discriminator: Rising feed-water-to-steam ratio (feed 2-3 t/h over steam) WITH boiler-water conductivity FALLING - the circuit is being diluted, which establishes a pressure-part leak and excludes every non-leak explanation of the water imbalance. Go observe (not in the six tags): boiler-water conductivity trend (falling = leak; rising = concentration / feed-control fault; a large CBD loss would also lower it); make-up water consumption rate; furnace listening check for a hissing steam leak; furnace draught stability (here fluctuating); local vs sharp bed temperature drop near the leak; whether drum level can still be held on one BFP. At inspection the fracture morphology (thin-lipped longitudinal split at a broadly thinned zone) confirms erosion over overheating or corrosion.

hypotheses.cause: Insufficient primary air velocity in one branch line after a PA damper was left throttled following maintenance, so the line dynamic pressure could no longer oppose the fluidised-bed static head and hot particles back-flowed and accumulated in the vertical portion. Systemic: no post-maintenance restoration checklist for damper positions, no compartment-wise PA flow measurement, and no PA line temperature monitoring.
hypotheses.discriminator: Confined to one compartment - the six-tag averages barely move. Go observe: PA flow to the affected compartment LOW while the PA header pressure stays NORMAL (isolates the restriction to that branch and excludes a fan/header cause); glowing hot material and rising surface temperature on the vertical portion of that PA line; erratic, non-uniform bed temperature in that one compartment only; bed differential pressure normal on all compartments (rules out excessive bed height); the bed ash drain valve verified closed and cold; the maintenance record showing recent work on that line with no damper restoration check.

hypotheses.cause: Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. Systemic: no cold-end metal temperature control or monitoring, no acid-dew-point recalculation after a fuel sulphur increase, and no periodic APH leakage measurement.
hypotheses.discriminator: Not visible in the six process tags except a slow bed-temperature drift over WEEKS (less effective primary air reaches the bed). Go observe: ESP inlet O2 RISING with no change in the combustion-air setting AND APH outlet flue gas temperature FALLING (the defining air-to-gas leakage pair); PA and SA fan motor current higher for the same delivered wind-box air flow (confirms an air-to-gas leak, not a duct-to-atmosphere leak); gas-side differential pressure across the APH NOT rising (rules out fouling); cold-end metal temperature vs the calculated acid dew point for the actual fuel sulphur; damage concentrated in the coldest rows with acidic corrosion products (vs erosion at the gas-entry face, vs fatigue at the tube sheets).

Distinguish from a fuel hang-up (Case 6) by the step-vs-ramp onset and by all compartments falling equally rather than compartment-selectively.

hypotheses.cause: Two independent failures in sequence: PA fan motor winding overheating from coal-dust fouling of the cooling air passages tripped the running fan, and a defective run feed-back contact aborted the standby PA fan auto-start. The combination removed all fluidising air, the bed defluidised, the feeders tripped on interlock and hot bed material migrated into the PA lines. Systemic: no scheduled motor cleaning for the known dusty environment and no periodic proof test of standby auto-start.
hypotheses.discriminator: Divergence between motor WINDING temperature (rising over ~30 min) and motor CURRENT (normal): an overload would raise current with temperature, an electrical fault would trip protection first, so a winding-temperature rise alone identifies loss of the cooling air path. Go observe (not in the six tags): PA fan motor winding temperature vs motor current trend; standby PA fan auto-start command present with no run feed-back (the hidden second failure); PA header pressure collapse and loss of primary air; all coal feeders tripping simultaneously on the designed PA-fan-trip interlock; erratic bed temperature indication and low furnace draught after fluidising air is lost. On the six averaged tags this looks the same as a total feeder loss (Case 14).

belief_ranking.cause: Insufficient primary air velocity in one branch line after a PA damper was left throttled following maintenance, so the line dynamic pressure could no longer oppose the fluidised-bed static head and hot particles back-flowed and accumulated in the vertical portion. Systemic: no post-maintenance restoration checklist for damper positions, no compartment-wise PA flow measurement, and no PA line temperature monitoring.

Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. Systemic: no cold-end metal temperature control or monitoring, no acid-dew-point recalculation after a fuel sulphur increase, and no periodic APH leakage measurement.

Loss of the HP heater and the resulting low economiser inlet feed water temperature, compensated by increased firing at constant load, exceeding the design single-stage attemperation capacity. Systemic: no operating rule linking HP heater unavailability to a mandatory load reduction and revised temperature-control strategy, plus an HP heater maintenance backlog.

Fireside erosion of a water wall tube by circulating bed material in the high-velocity bed-to-freeboard transition zone, progressively thinning the wall until it split longitudinally; internal deposits contributed by raising local metal temperature. Systemic: a foreseeable wear-out mechanism with no thickness-monitoring task, wear shields removed without engineering review, and an uncontrolled operating envelope (excess air, bed height, ash abrasiveness).

Loss of a stable light-up flame from degraded atomisation - water and sediment in the LDO choked the burner nozzle, with low atomising steam pressure and marginal combustion air, so the flame could not sustain itself; a separately developing photocell fouling added a false loss-of-flame indication. Systemic: the whole light-up system is standby equipment maintained reactively, so multiple hidden failures accumulated and appeared together on demand.

Deflagration on re-ignition of an accumulated un-burnt fuel-air mixture, made possible by a passing oil-burner shut-off valve and by omission of the mandatory purge. Systemic: a safety-critical interlock (purge permissive) could be defeated by a single operator without authorisation or review, within a management system that tolerated known passing fuel valves and repeated flame failures as routine.

Bed temperature runaway to the sintering range from loss of the ash recirculation cooling and bed-inventory path, combined with an uncompensated increase in fuel calorific value and a partially choked PA line reducing fluidising air on the affected compartments. Systemic: no proceduralised combustion re-setting for fuel property changes (no ash-fusion testing on receipt), and the safety-relevant ash recirculation system neither alarmed nor monitored.

Fail-to-open of the PRDS dumping control valve on demand, so the designed pressure-relief route was unavailable during a foreseeable turbine trip, compounded by a delayed manual fuel cutback against the thermal inertia of the fluidised bed. Systemic: no periodic in-service proof test of the dumping valve, and no automatic fuel-runback / bed-slumping interlock on turbine trip.

Systemic: no scheduled motor cleaning for the known dusty environment and no periodic proof test of standby auto-start.
hypotheses.discriminator: Divergence between motor WINDING temperature (rising over ~30 min) and motor CURRENT (normal): an overload would raise current with temperature, an electrical fault would trip protection first, so a winding-temperature rise alone identifies loss of the cooling air path. Go observe (not in the six tags): PA fan motor winding temperature vs motor current trend; standby PA fan auto-start command present with no run feed-back (the hidden second failure); PA header pressure collapse and loss of primary air; all coal feeders tripping simultaneously on the designed PA-fan-trip interlock; erratic bed temperature indication and low furnace draught after fluidising air is lost. On the six averaged tags this looks the same as a total feeder loss (Case 14).

belief_ranking.cause: Insufficient primary air velocity in one branch line after a PA damper was left throttled following maintenance, so the line dynamic pressure could no longer oppose the fluidised-bed static head and hot particles back-flowed and accumulated in the vertical portion. Systemic: no post-maintenance restoration checklist for damper positions, no compartment-wise PA flow measurement, and no PA line temperature monitoring.

Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. Systemic: no cold-end metal temperature control or monitoring, no acid-dew-point recalculation after a fuel sulphur increase, and no periodic APH leakage measurement.

Loss of the HP heater and the resulting low economiser inlet feed water temperature, compensated by increased firing at constant load, exceeding the design single-stage attemperation capacity. Systemic: no operating rule linking HP heater unavailability to a mandatory load reduction and revised temperature-control strategy, plus an HP heater maintenance backlog.

Fireside erosion of a water wall tube by circulating bed material in the high-velocity bed-to-freeboard transition zone, progressively thinning the wall until it split longitudinally; internal deposits contributed by raising local metal temperature. Systemic: a foreseeable wear-out mechanism with no thickness-monitoring task, wear shields removed without engineering review, and an uncontrolled operating envelope (excess air, bed height, ash abrasiveness).

Loss of a stable light-up flame from degraded atomisation - water and sediment in the LDO choked the burner nozzle, with low atomising steam pressure and marginal combustion air, so the flame could not sustain itself; a separately developing photocell fouling added a false loss-of-flame indication. Systemic: the whole light-up system is standby equipment maintained reactively, so multiple hidden failures accumulated and appeared together on demand.

Deflagration on re-ignition of an accumulated un-burnt fuel-air mixture, made possible by a passing oil-burner shut-off valve and by omission of the mandatory purge. Systemic: a safety-critical interlock (purge permissive) could be defeated by a single operator without authorisation or review, within a management system that tolerated known passing fuel valves and repeated flame failures as routine.

Bed temperature runaway to the sintering range from loss of the ash recirculation cooling and bed-inventory path, combined with an uncompensated increase in fuel calorific value and a partially choked PA line reducing fluidising air on the affected compartments. Systemic: no proceduralised combustion re-setting for fuel property changes (no ash-fusion testing on receipt), and the safety-relevant ash recirculation system neither alarmed nor monitored.

Fail-to-open of the PRDS dumping control valve on demand, so the designed pressure-relief route was unavailable during a foreseeable turbine trip, compounded by a delayed manual fuel cutback against the thermal inertia of the fluidised bed. Systemic: no periodic in-service proof test of the dumping valve, and no automatic fuel-runback / bed-slumping interlock on turbine trip.

hypotheses.discriminator: Rising feed-water-to-steam ratio (feed 2-3 t/h over steam) WITH boiler-water conductivity FALLING - the circuit is being diluted, which establishes a pressure-part leak and excludes every non-leak explanation of the water imbalance. Go observe (not in the six tags): boiler-water conductivity trend (falling = leak; rising = concentration / feed-control fault; a large CBD loss would also lower it); make-up water consumption rate; furnace listening check for a hissing steam leak; furnace draught stability (here fluctuating); local vs sharp bed temperature drop near the leak; whether drum level can still be held on one BFP. At inspection the fracture morphology (thin-lipped longitudinal split at a broadly thinned zone) confirms erosion over overheating or corrosion.

hypotheses.cause: Insufficient primary air velocity in one branch line after a PA damper was left throttled following maintenance, so the line dynamic pressure could no longer oppose the fluidised-bed static head and hot particles back-flowed and accumulated in the vertical portion. hypotheses.discriminator: Confined to one compartment - the six-tag averages barely move. Go observe: PA flow to the affected compartment LOW while the PA header pressure stays NORMAL (isolates the restriction to that branch and excludes a fan/header cause); glowing hot material and rising surface temperature on the vertical portion of that PA line; erratic, non-uniform bed temperature in that one compartment only; bed differential pressure normal on all compartments (rules out excessive bed height); the bed ash drain valve verified closed and cold; the maintenance record showing recent work on that line with no damper restoration check.

hypotheses.cause: Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. hypotheses.discriminator: Not visible in the six process tags except a slow bed-temperature drift over WEEKS (less effective primary air reaches the bed). Go observe: ESP inlet O2 RISING with no change in the combustion-air setting AND APH outlet flue gas temperature FALLING (the defining air-to-gas leakage pair); PA and SA fan motor current higher for the same delivered wind-box air flow (confirms an air-to-gas leak, not a duct-to-atmosphere leak); gas-side differential pressure across the APH NOT rising (rules out fouling); cold-end metal temperature vs the calculated acid dew point for the actual fuel sulphur; damage concentrated in the coldest rows with acidic corrosion products (vs erosion at the gas-entry face, vs fatigue at the tube sheets).

Systemic: a foreseeable wear-out mechanism with no thickness-monitoring task, wear shields removed without engineering review, and an uncontrolled operating envelope (excess air, bed height, ash abrasiveness).
hypotheses.discriminator: Rising feed-water-to-steam ratio (feed 2-3 t/h over steam) WITH boiler-water conductivity FALLING - the circuit is being diluted, which establishes a pressure-part leak and excludes every non-leak explanation of the water imbalance. Go observe (not in the six tags): boiler-water conductivity trend (falling = leak; rising = concentration / feed-control fault; a large CBD loss would also lower it); make-up water consumption rate; furnace listening check for a hissing steam leak; furnace draught stability (here fluctuating); local vs sharp bed temperature drop near the leak; whether drum level can still be held on one BFP. At inspection the fracture morphology (thin-lipped longitudinal split at a broadly thinned zone) confirms erosion over overheating or corrosion.

hypotheses.cause: Insufficient primary air velocity in one branch line after a PA damper was left throttled following maintenance, so the line dynamic pressure could no longer oppose the fluidised-bed static head and hot particles back-flowed and accumulated in the vertical portion. Systemic: no post-maintenance restoration checklist for damper positions, no compartment-wise PA flow measurement, and no PA line temperature monitoring.
hypotheses.discriminator: Confined to one compartment - the six-tag averages barely move. Go observe: PA flow to the affected compartment LOW while the PA header pressure stays NORMAL (isolates the restriction to that branch and excludes a fan/header cause); glowing hot material and rising surface temperature on the vertical portion of that PA line; erratic, non-uniform bed temperature in that one compartment only; bed differential pressure normal on all compartments (rules out excessive bed height); the bed ash drain valve verified closed and cold; the maintenance record showing recent work on that line with no damper restoration check.

hypotheses.cause: Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. Systemic: no cold-end metal temperature control or monitoring, no acid-dew-point recalculation after a fuel sulphur increase, and no periodic APH leakage measurement.
hypotheses.discriminator: Not visible in the six process tags except a slow bed-temperature drift over WEEKS (less effective primary air reaches the bed). Go observe: ESP inlet O2 RISING with no change in the combustion-air setting AND APH outlet flue gas temperature FALLING (the defining air-to-gas leakage pair); PA and SA fan motor current higher for the same delivered wind-box air flow (confirms an air-to-gas leak, not a duct-to-atmosphere leak); gas-side differential pressure across the APH NOT rising (rules out fouling); cold-end metal temperature vs the calculated acid dew point for the actual fuel sulphur; damage concentrated in the coldest rows with acidic corrosion products (vs erosion at the gas-entry face, vs fatigue at the tube sheets).

actions.text: Check make-up water consumption rate and inspect furnace for audible steam leak from a safe position
Reduce load in consultation with the shift in-charge until the cause is identified
Prepare for manual feed control and keep the standby feed path available

hypotheses.cause: Total loss of fuel input from a degraded connection on one phase of the MCC incomer producing single-phasing, tripping all six coal feeder VFDs on phase loss. Systemic: all six feeders on one un-segregated bus section (a single-point-of-failure), and an electrical PM programme with no thermography and no connection-torque verification.
hypotheses.discriminator: All six feeder drives reporting an incoming supply abnormality (phase loss / under-voltage) at the same instant. Simultaneity across six independent mechanical drives is near-conclusive for a supply-side common cause, and the VFD fault-code content separates it from a process interlock, an operator stop and a drive-internal fault. Go observe (not in the six tags): the six VFD fault codes and their timestamps; the MCC incomer protection operation in the electrical event log; absence of any preceding bed temperature / drum level / furnace pressure excursion (process interlocks leave a clear trend trace); PA fan status (here running normally); DCS operator command logs (no stop command). Distinguish from a fuel hang-up (Case 6) by the step-vs-ramp onset and by all compartments falling equally rather than compartment-selectively.

hypotheses.cause: Two independent failures in sequence: PA fan motor winding overheating from coal-dust fouling of the cooling air passages tripped the running fan, and a defective run feed-back contact aborted the standby PA fan auto-start. The combination removed all fluidising air, the bed defluidised, the feeders tripped on interlock and hot bed material migrated into the PA lines. Systemic: no scheduled motor cleaning for the known dusty environment and no periodic proof test of standby auto-start.
hypotheses.discriminator: Divergence between motor WINDING temperature (rising over ~30 min) and motor CURRENT (normal): an overload would raise current with temperature, an electrical fault would trip protection first, so a winding-temperature rise alone identifies loss of the cooling air path. Go observe (not in the six tags): PA fan motor winding temperature vs motor current trend; standby PA fan auto-start command present with no run feed-back (the hidden second failure); PA header pressure collapse and loss of primary air; all coal feeders tripping simultaneously on the designed PA-fan-trip interlock; erratic bed temperature indication and low furnace draught after fluidising air is lost. On the six averaged tags this looks the same as a total feeder loss (Case 14).

Sulphuric acid condensation on cold-end APH tube surfaces running below the acid dew point, causing progressive external wall loss and perforation, with ash erosion at the tube inlets as a secondary contributor. Systemic: no cold-end metal temperature control or monitoring, no acid-dew-point recalculation after a fuel sulphur increase, and no periodic APH leakage measurement.

Loss of the HP heater and the resulting low economiser inlet feed water temperature, compensated by increased firing at constant load, exceeding the design single-stage attemperation capacity. Systemic: no operating rule linking HP heater unavailability to a mandatory load reduction and revised temperature-control strategy, plus an HP heater maintenance backlog.

Fireside erosion of a water wall tube by circulating bed material in the high-velocity bed-to-freeboard transition zone, progressively thinning the wall until it split longitudinally; internal deposits contributed by raising local metal temperature. Systemic: a foreseeable wear-out mechanism with no thickness-monitoring task, wear shields removed without engineering review, and an uncontrolled operating envelope (excess air, bed height, ash abrasiveness).

Loss of a stable light-up flame from degraded atomisation - water and sediment in the LDO choked the burner nozzle, with low atomising steam pressure and marginal combustion air, so the flame could not sustain itself; a separately developing photocell fouling added a false loss-of-flame indication. Systemic: the whole light-up system is standby equipment maintained reactively, so multiple hidden failures accumulated and appeared together on demand.

Deflagration on re-ignition of an accumulated un-burnt fuel-air mixture, made possible by a passing oil-burner shut-off valve and by omission of the mandatory purge. Systemic: a safety-critical interlock (purge permissive) could be defeated by a single operator without authorisation or review, within a management system that tolerated known passing fuel valves and repeated flame failures as routine.

Bed temperature runaway to the sintering range from loss of the ash recirculation cooling and bed-inventory path, combined with an uncompensated increase in fuel calorific value and a partially choked PA line reducing fluidising air on the affected compartments. Systemic: no proceduralised combustion re-setting for fuel property changes (no ash-fusion testing on receipt), and the safety-relevant ash recirculation system neither alarmed nor monitored.

Fail-to-open of the PRDS dumping control valve on demand, so the designed pressure-relief route was unavailable during a foreseeable turbine trip, compounded by a delayed manual fuel cutback against the thermal inertia of the fluidised bed. Systemic: no periodic in-service proof test of the dumping valve, and no automatic fuel-runback / bed-slumping interlock on turbine trip.
